utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Meek and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, presents is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I don't see the witness. I take it there are some preliminaries, then, or -- yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received two documents on the -- in the archives -- regarding the archives of the Drina Corps. We received the document yesterday, and I would like to ask for additional cross-examination of the witness who was already here and will come back, Mr. Blaszczyk. And I need about 15 to 20 minutes, if possible. That's the first thing. And second thing, if we could please move to private session, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session, if you could kindly respond to Madam Fauveau, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't object to that. What happened is you may recall when Mr. Blaszczyk was testifying, he said he had heard something like from another team or something about someone that had looked into the Drina Corps collection. So we asked around and we found an investigator that had made some requests to Serbia and the RS about the collection and got back some responses. It's nothing that I saw was very new, but when we got it we turned it over. So that's what that is about. We didn't of course speak to Mr. Blaszczyk at all about any of it. We just heard what he said and asked around and found some material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to have about 20 minutes of cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are always in the unfortunate position of not having seen these documents and then have to consider submissions like the one you make and the one Mr. McCloskey responds with, that there is nothing new in these documents. So let's think about it and then we'll come back to you, Madam Fauveau. All right. Anything else? Let's bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, sorry. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. We are hopefully going to finish with your testimony today. Mr. Ostojic still has a few minutes more. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we left off discussing really your diary in -- I was trying to find the page where I felt that there was an entry. So maybe we can start quickly by going into private session, and I referenced it yesterday at page 134, and so I could ask you a couple of questions about that, please. So if we can go into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We are not yet. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about what's been referred to in various literature and books as the Bosnian Muslim spring or summer offensive of 1995. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for our transcript we need to have your verbal response?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But thank you very much. And when did that Bosnian Muslim offensive in the spring or summer of 1995 commence?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, when I landed in Sarajevo, on May 15th, 1995, it had started a day or two earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you share with us the nature and extent of that Bosnian Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were trying to break out of the strangle around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it limited to Sarajevo only?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, when it started, at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you P2970, if you don't mind. And do you remember, sir, page 3, when you get a chance, I'll put the question to the witness. Do you remember that there was a significant increase in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what this document is off the top of my head and it's not on any list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour, 65 ter number P2970 as being on the list of documents provided by the Office of the Prosecution for this particular witness. So I can't imagine that they don't know what the document is. It's on their list. I can put this on the ELMO if the Court needs assistance. And it doesn't have a P number, but it says 65 ter 2970 and it has the ERN number, it's rather long, R 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: R 002-4213 through R 002-4218 in the English version. I can recite the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you can't expect the Prosecution to divine what documents you're using unless you announce beforehand what documents you will be using.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: These are their documents that they provided that they were going to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you expect Mr. Thayer or anyone for that matter to know the thousands of documents that have a 65 ter number by heart and be able to distinguish them by number as soon as they appear on the screen? This is the whole point that has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see the point. It's actually eight documents that they identify with this witness. I thought that they would have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move. Let's move now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I inquire of this document, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a weekly situation report that's dated the 2nd of July 1995 from David Harland, a similar type weekly situation report that you discussed during your direct examination, and I direct your attention - or at least for my next question - on page 3 which was in essence, do you recall that in June of 1995 there was a significant increase in the Bosnian heavy weapons operating from near UNPROFOR facilities?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you just remember that, first?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how significant was the increase?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, significant in that as far as I recall, and that's still quite early in my tour, they hadn't been doing it before, and heavy weapons we are referring to roadblock probably light mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be considered heavy weapons, light mortars?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well for the purpose of a weapon collection point, no, but compared to everything that he had in their hands, it was I guess the Heaviest at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, sir, when you were there in June and July of 1995, whether the Bosnian Muslims were trying to draw UNPROFOR into the conflict against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We felt that they tried at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, whether or not that happened in June of 1995 as well as July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have to look at the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have no recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't comment generally like that but as I said, it did happen at times, but we can go through the various occasions, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we will hopefully. Now, on page 3, there, on the bottom it says, "Location of Bosnian weapons a problem." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This was also a report by David Harland, and I think with his other weekly situation reports, you would have found it was useful reliable and accurate, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well looking at this did you review this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So this isn't a surprise to you, this document, right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in this section in particular that raises any concern that it may be inaccurate to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is drawing my attention and he's absolutely right, that you're going too fast. Please allow a short break between question -- a short pause between question and answer. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat the question, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So are you in a position to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just reading the text, Your Honour and then translation switched to French in my ear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure that that didn't irritate you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. Is there anything in this section in particular that has raised any concern to you that it may be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the second paragraph under this section, "Location of Bosnian weapons a problem," it identifies that some people in UNPROFOR see this, meaning the significant increase in heavy weapons, as an effort by the Bosnians to draw counterbattery fire on to UNPROFOR, do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What do they mean when they say some people in UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess not everyone agreed with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who did, do you know?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about in this occasion on July 2nd of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It goes on in that sentence to say that, "It would then be drawn into conflict with the Serbs." That would mean that UNPROFOR would be drawn into a conflict with the Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir just --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to talk also a little bit about propaganda at that time. In July 1992, as you sit here, do you recall any of the propaganda that was going on by the Bosnian government against the Serbs in connection with the war that was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1995. Thank you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned yesterday, there was propaganda, as in any war from all sides, but I can't recall specifics off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, sir, at any point in July of 1995, whether the situation with respect to the propaganda began to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. For example, if the Bosnian Muslims started to increase their political pressure on UNPROFOR by giving out statements against UNPROFOR and saying that they were complicit with the Serbs in various activities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read that again. Well, things like that happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember it happening in July of 1995 immediately after the Bosnian Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any specific occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's look at the next page of this document, if you will. It talks about UNPROFOR's relations with the Bosnian government deteriorating. Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's highlighted and then there is some paragraphs beneath. And you've read this section as you shared with us in preparation for your testimony here. Do you remember that the Prime Minister was actually criticising the United Nations and saying that they were an accomplice in a genocide against Bosnia on or about June 26th, 1995? It's in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm. I'm reading. Yes. I do not recall this particular situation, but as I said things like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What were they referencing when they said this complicit genocide in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, just going back quickly to this increase -- significant increase in heavy weapons, do you know if there was such an increase in heavy weapons also in the Srebrenica enclave on or near July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the events, Srebrenica, around the 8, 9, 10 of July, there was an increase, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it a significant increase?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, the Bosnian military in Srebrenica were defending themselves against an attack by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But was there a significant increase in the heavy weapons in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what weapons were significantly increased in that enclave in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure but I would suspect they would be light mortars which we did not control in WCPs like other heavier weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what other heavier weapons did you have within the WCPs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica itself, I don't recall because I was not involved in Srebrenica except for those three or four days, but generally they were heavy mortars, artillery, and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you, sir, remember that the Bosnian Muslims provoked a situation in Srebrenica by killing a DutchBat soldier?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What situation did they provoke?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The escalation of combat there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they did kill a Dutch soldier. I wouldn't say it provoked an escalation in combat but it complicated the situation for the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Muslims complicate the situation for the Dutch in any other way other than by that, by killing a DutchBat soldier, although you're not sure of it but we will get to that in a second?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I recall is they were siting some of their weapons near the TACP operated by British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how did that hamper the situation for DutchBat or the civilians there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for DutchBat, if they site their weapons near the TACP and fire on the Serbs with those weapons, when the Serbs fire back, they can hit the TACP so it has to move, and when it moves it did cannot do it its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that also hamper the task of controlling of the close air support if any was ordered at that time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's basically what I mean when I say could not do its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's -- if I can direct your attention to Exhibit 6D152, which I think the Prosecutor has which is your November 1997 statement that you gave to them, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention, if I may, to page 17 for the moment. Now, just to clarify in that third paragraph there, although it's the third sentence, it states that "The Bosnians fired and a Dutch soldier was wounded in the head and later died." End quote. Do you see that? Third paragraph, third sentence, I believe?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fourth sentence actually. This is your statement. Is there any doubt in your mind that the Bosnians fired at the Dutch soldiers and wounded this Dutch soldier and ultimately killed him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's how it was reported by the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then it also says there was damage to a Dutch vehicle by the Bosnian Muslims, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that was -- how was that vehicle damaged, do you know?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was there any investigation done on that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it because there -- they didn't withdrew under Serb pressure to the compound in Potocari, and I don't think they had much time to start to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, it lists these three or four things, the killing of the Dutch soldier, the damage to the Dutch vehicle, the attraction of fire to the TACPs by situating weapons close to it, hampering its risk of controlling the close air support or CAS, then it goes on to say, and I think it's your superior insisted, is that Gobillard, how do you say his name?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He insisted that the Bosnians be told that the act of their soldiers was tantamount to a murder. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was he referencing all four or so of the things listed above?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killing of the Dutch soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was the only thing he referenced?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, whether General Nicolai had at any time talked to Tolimir in order to secure the Serbian cooperation for the evacuation of the Dutch soldier killed by the Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember he talked to someone on the Serb side, I believe it was Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are talking about this provocation, and if you can tell me whether or not there was further provocation other than this instance that we've identified, or these instances that is we've identified on page 17 of your witness statement, which occurred on or about July 8th of 1995 and that would have been again, just to briefly refresh your recollection, the killing of the Dutch soldier, the attack on the Dutch vehicle, et cetera. Were there other provocations or instances where the Bosnian Muslims provoked or attacked DutchBat or any members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, whether or not two days after this incident, the Bosnian Muslims were firing at DutchBat who were with drawing from their observation posts?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if you need to read all I'm asking if you remember, if you don't I'll direct your attention to the next page which is page 18 where in your witness statement, in the middle of it, with the caption starting on July 10th, which is two days after this one, it discusses a meeting that was conducted and that there was a surprise at the ABiH reaction that they had fired at withdrawing Dutch forces. And it's the fourth full paragraph, if you see that in the middle of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Does it help refresh your recollection that in fact there was a surprise by UNPROFOR that the Bosnian Muslims, despite what happened on the 8th of July 1995, two days later they continued and fired at withdrawing DutchBat soldiers, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure they are one and the same events that are being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know they are not the same events, sir. And that's why my question preceding that was do you know of any others incidents where the Bosnian Muslims provoked or attacked DutchBat other than the instances that we described on July 8th. And so we have also this on July 10th, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's your witness statement. Do you doubt it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not that I doubt it. It's I can't remember every single word I wrote ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you should, sir. Also do you remember, sir, as you sit here whether or not the Bosnian Muslims prevented a resupply to the Ukrainians in Zepa in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They made it more difficult. I remember then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were blocking the OPs, the Ukrainians OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about resupply first. So were they in fact preventing resupply and preventing all resupply to the Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details. As I said, I remember they were blocking. By blocking the OPs you prevent anything going in, including resupply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember whether the Bosnian Muslims not only blocked those OPs but also attacked them?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well in what cases do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how many observation posts were there in Zepa that the Ukrainians were manning?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the Bosnian Muslims attacked the Ukrainian observation posts at -- observation post 1, 5, 7, and 8?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think I wrote that much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So let's look at page 20 of your report, if you don't mind. And the actual first full paragraph, after the numeric 3, the second-to-last sentence it says, "In Zepa the Bosnians were preventing all resupply of the Ukrainians." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you could just -- if this helps refresh your recollection, from whom did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From, I believe from the Ukrainians themselves, in the early stages of the incidents at Zepa and throughout, we were in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you say, "preventing all resupply," can you tell me what that entails?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, food, water, fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, why -- anything else?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are the basic commodities that you need on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well did the Ukrainians have any weapons or anything else that they may have needed other than food, water and fuel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had weapons but they were not shooting them, so there is no need to resupply bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the Bosnian Muslims were preventing all resupply of the Ukrainians in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that was a practice at all in Srebrenica as well by the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, down below on that same page 20 of your witness statement from November of 1997, the last paragraph identifies July 14th as the next date.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so, sir, we are on the same page we talked about the 8th of July. We talked about the 10th of July. And then I believe that the situation where there was a prevention of supplies to the Ukrainians was occurring, at least according to your statement, on or about the 12th of July, and then two days later again there was information that was provided to you, since you identified in your report, that the Bosnians had attacked the Ukrainian observation posts. Do you see that? It's in the middle of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well the -- as it's written there, on July 14 we were informed by the Ukrainian deputy sector commander. It doesn't say that two days after the 12th or July 14th, that they attacked again. It said that we were informed that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But keep reading, sir, it says also later that evening --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you keep reading in that paragraph, sir, although I do take your point, and I wish you to take mine, it says "later that same evening." What evening do you think you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 14th, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when -- but he says later that evening on the 14th, which is clear, you were informed that the Bosnians had attacked the Ukrainian observation posts, 1, 5, 7 and 8, right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So do you think that the observation posts were attacked by the Bosnian Muslims before July 14th?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that sentence refers to July 14th, that is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw it that way too, sir. Do you know why it is that the Bosnian Muslims attacked the Ukrainian observation or UNPROFOR observation posts on July 14th 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure why they would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever investigate it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally investigate it and things happening so fast at that time that we don't have time to chase every loose end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, sir. Do you know if there were any other provocations or instances where the Bosnian Muslims attacked or hindered the work of UNPROFOR in Zepa in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you remember a meeting with General Smith and President Izetbegovic to discuss UNPROFOR's assistance in the evacuation of the population in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You already yesterday asked him whether General Smith ever met with Izetbegovic and he answered that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If this is supposedly another meeting, it would still fall under the previous answer that he gave you. But if he's thought about it and has got fresh information, then he can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay let's take a look at page 21 of your witness, if you don't mind, you identify in your witness statement the conversation, and you identified that Smith then went to Izetbegovic, and it's on page 21, second-to-the-last paragraph. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I said, General Smith may have told people at a meeting that I was present that he did that, but I was not present at the meeting that he had with Izetbegovic or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How do you draw in your statement sir the following, if you weren't at the meeting, and seemingly may not know anything about it as follows: "Smith then went to Izetbegovic to discuss UNPROFOR assistance in the evacuation of the population."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he told us so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you knew that he met with Izetbegovic to discuss UNPROFOR's assistance in the evacuation of the population, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that that had happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you as well?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know -- but he told General Gobillard, and I was with Gobillard, but I don't know. I was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you were at the meeting but you have information about it. Could you share with us -- I'm just pausing so that I don't go too fast for the translators. Can you share with us why it was that General Smith went to Izetbegovic to discuss what UNPROFOR's assistance would be if any with the evacuation of the population?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here, do you know if Smith was required to obtain Izetbegovic's approval or authorisation for UNPROFOR to assist in the evacuation of the population?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he needed his authorisation, but there was a need for example to discuss a global prisoner exchange, and so the Bosnian government was a party in that negotiation. That may have been the -- these things had to be sorted out in order for UNPROFOR to go further in its assistance so that may have been what was discussed, but I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. You said that and thank you for repeating it for me, but this is an event that is occurring on the 19th of July 1995. It doesn't discuss at all the prisoner of war exchange, it doesn't discuss exchange in a global level, all it does is talk about UNPROFOR's assistance for the evacuation of the population, does it not?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. That's what it says. But these -- these events were happening at the same time. They are not all reported in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, whether the Bosnian Muslims were seeking a firm guarantee for their safety from UNPROFOR during any of the meetings you may have attended or have been briefed upon?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share that with me. What part in July was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the meeting in Zepa, that I attended, when I was there on July 27th, I believe it was, Mladic was trying to obtain an agreement with the three Bosnian civilian representatives of Zepa, and UNPROFOR had guarantees to offer for that agreement to be valid, and we could not guarantee those.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what -- what were those guarantees that Mladic was purportedly seeking for UNPROFOR to offer?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ensure the security of the evacuees, I think was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What was the other one?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, whose job was it to secure the population and this enclave in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I'm -- the evacuees, meaning while they were being transported out, we didn't have the means to move them out and the Serbs did, buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR provide any fuel for that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the guarantee that the -- was it the guarantee that Mladic wanted or the Bosnian Muslims wanted, that there be security and that they be provided with security during the evacuation process?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who wanted it, but it was essential for the agreement, in our view, any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think there is any doubt that the Bosnian Muslims wanted to have UNPROFOR secure that they have safe passage as they were evacuating from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can just direct your attention briefly to page 25 of your witness statement, sir, it's the second full paragraph. And was the deal or the offer to provide security to the evacuees based on any other part of an agreement. Or was it as you say just a fact that UNPROFOR didn't have the capacity, if you will to do that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Look at -- you reviewed this prior to testimony -- in preparation for your testimony, the second full paragraph, and towards the middle of that paragraph it talks about "As for the Bosnian army, then Tolimir suggests or indicated that they were ready to surrender and drop their weapons provided that they could obtain firm guarantees, which is what we talked about, for their safe -- for their safety from UNPROFOR," which you told us you couldn't give, the very next sentence is what I would like to discuss with you. It seems here that you and your superior did not provide these guarantees because you were more concerned with the global POW exchange agreement. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was part of the whole package.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What were some of the other parts, sir, and then we'll go through them?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the civilians were to be evacuated to Kladanj and the Serbs wanted the males of military age under their custody, and in order for us to have some guarantees that they would be safe in Serb custody we needed a global prisoner exchange agreement so that there was a way for those people to go back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, wasn't one of the things that the Bosnian Serbs were offering was that ICRC could come in and actually register each and every one of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the response of UNPROFOR to that? Inadequate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR is not ICRC. We can't decide for them but they have to be involved and I'm not sure, I didn't play any part in discussions with the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, from time to time, you worked with the ICRC, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met some people of the ICRC, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I did not work with the ICRC on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, do you find it or did you find it in July of 1995 inadequate for the Bosnian Serbs to offer that ICRC can come in under the supervision of UNPROFOR and register all the people that were to be detained as POWs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I find that inadequate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Thank you, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I take it you are next, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. We'll have the break in half an hour's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Colonel, my name is David Josse, and with the gentlemen who sits to my left, we defend General Gvero. I would like to begin by taking you back to the 28th of July of 1995 and your presence in Zepa. As far as you were concerned, on that day, who was in charge of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you see him there that day?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the 28th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And who, as far as you could see, was assisting General Mladic in that regard?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that a little later on, if I may. How competent was General Gobillard's English?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very much. That's why I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you present when he had conversations in English with either General Nicolai or General Smith?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say most of the time I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Bad question. I meant on occasions. That's really what I wanted to ascertain. I take it from what you just said, the answer is that, yes you were there on occasions when Gobillard spoke to Smith and/or Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there most of the time. I wouldn't say on occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. What language were such conversations conducted in?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Gobillard's English was good enough to cope with that type of meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could understand quite a bit, but he had difficulty speaking the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when he tried to express himself, what would he do? Use French and you would translate for him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You presumably spoke to him in French. You personally.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get to speak to him very much but yes, in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you present when General Janvier had meetings with English speakers or perhaps I should say non-French speakers?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he came to Sarajevo and had meetings in Sector Sarajevo headquarters, in those cases General Gobillard would have been present and I would have been present. In other cases, no, I worked for Gobillard and not for General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so can you recall ever being present at a meeting between General Janvier, Gobillard, and Smith?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I don't recall any particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not a -- it's not a trick question, and if you don't recall, I don't think you're going to be able to answer my follow-up question which was to do with the language used, and whether you could comment on General Janvier's competence in English. Can you assist on that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall his personal competence, but he also had people like me who could help him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any of UNPROFOR generals at any stage during your tenure in Bosnia handing small gifts to any of the generals of the warring parties, any of the three warring parties? For example, a regimental plaque, bottle of liquor, something like that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's certainly not something that happened often as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you briefly, in your statement, I don't think I need to take you to it in this regard, you mention quite early, I think, in your stay in Bosnia, going to Gorazde and you had a General Walker with you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember his Christian name?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: British, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his role in Bosnia, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the allied rapid reaction corps who -- that corps would take up the bulk of responsibility as IFOR eventually, so he was coming for what we call a recce.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or a recon, if you're American.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in your brief dealing with him, presumably you found him to be a competent officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly judge. Generals tend to talk to other generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know if you're aware, but he in fact ended up chief of Defence in the United Kingdom, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm now going to take you, if I may, to the conversation that you translated in part between General Gobillard and my client, General Gvero, on the 11th of July of 1995. Before I look at the actual documentation with you, you have already confirmed that this conversation was taking place through some sort of double translation. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, where was General Gvero physically at the time General Gobillard was talking to him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No idea at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were translating everything for General Gobillard; is that correct? Or was he able to understand a bit of the conversation in English?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to understand quite a bit. It's replying that was more difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So -- and this is important, the specifics here, if you can remember. Did you translate everything for him into French or was he able to understand some of what the English interpreter was saying?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to understand some of what she was saying, but he would often in those cases double check with me to make sure he got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of grammar or the such like, do you recall how good was the English of the Serbian English translator?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As good as yours, sir. She was British.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: She was British. And you presumably don't know where this woman was situated, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was right beside me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: She was beside you. And General Gobillard -- I beg your pardon, General Gvero had an interpreter as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. The interpretation that I used was the one that was done on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the name of your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think her name was Bliss, Captain Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about her later on in a different context. But she, as you say, was a British officer, and she was a liaison officer, wasn't she, one of General Smith's liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So she was beside you throughout this conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, as I say, we will look at the intercept, at the document in a moment, but General Gvero made reference to a Svetlana. Do you remember that? If you don't I'll help you by showing you a document?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What we're going to do now is show you the actual -- your note, which is P2968. We're also going to show you another document, P2379 and before they are brought up, Your Honour, what we've done, because this is going to be quite a long and cumbersome exercise, we have produced English copies of both of these for the witness and for the Bench because otherwise this is going to be, as I say, quite a messy exercise. I would respectfully suggest that on e-court the B/C/S versions are put up so that the accused can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that okay with you, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I take it that when we refer to English copies we are referring to the actual report of the conversation that's been marked as 2968 on the one hand as well as the English translation that's in e-court of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to explain to the witness what 2379 is so that he's aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For us, I think it will be useful to have the texts that Mr. Josse has just -- and I think it will be useful for the witness to have those as well because otherwise I take Mr. Josse's word that it will become cumbersome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I believe that's intercept 2374, not 2379 if we are talking about the 1610, or are we talking about the subsequent one at 1810?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The one that involves this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, can I explain to you, Colonel, what 2379 is? Before I do that, one other thing. I don't know whether there is any problem, Your Honour, with 2379 being broadcast. Perhaps Madam Registrar could advise on that. 2379 is an English translation of a purported intercept made by the Muslim security services at the time that your conversation with General Gvero was taking place, or perhaps I should say General Gobillard's conversation with General Gvero. The intercept operator, as is clear from the first paragraph, could only hear General Gvero. He could not hear your end of the conversation at all. And my first question to you is have you been shown this before?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware, prior to this moment, that the conversation had in some way been intercepted by a security force?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was advised that an intercept existed but not by whom it was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were advised that during the course of your proofing, were you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you weren't actually shown the documents?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the other thing I should tell you and it's an obvious point the original of 2379 is of course in the B/C/S language, not in the English language. This is a translation. And dealing with the point that I was just asking you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. 2379, I'm informed, is under seal. So no broadcast of it, please. Otherwise, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we look quite near the top of this conversation, which I'm going to take you to in a moment, we see that Gvero says, "Hello, this is Gvero." Then he says, "Who?" Then he says, "Svetlana". And then if we look at the bottom of that very same page, we see him, Gvero, saying, "Don't let him start talking while I'm talking. Svetlana, could you please translate to General Gobillard?" So what I'm suggesting to you is General Gobillard -- General Gvero had an interpreter there called Svetlana. Does this help you at all in that regard?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm suggesting is that Gvero had an interpreter, somewhere at his end, called Svetlana.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And assuming that to be correct, what I'd like you to try and explain is the interplay between Gvero, Svetlana, Captain Bliss, yourself, and General Gobillard. How did it work?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that part. I don't remember a Svetlana.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you tell us, Colonel, how the conversation worked, physically worked, as far as you're concerned. I don't think the intercept will help you in this regard. We are going to look at it in a few moments' time.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, the interpreter would talk to General Gvero in Serbo-Croatian. He would reply, she would translate to me in English. I would translate to General Gobillard in French. He would give me his reply in French. I would tell it in English to the interpreter. And she would then translate for the person at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the interpreter you are referring to is Captain Bliss?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure it was Captain Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've got no idea about a Svetlana?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And by the same token, you presumably would have no idea whether -- well, I'll suggest to you, you probably don't know this, that Svetlana was in fact physically in a different location to General Gvero, just to complicate matters. But you don't know that, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Bearing in mind your role which you've just described, Colonel, how were you able to note the conversation down? Tell us physically how you did that.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it was -- in between my interpretation with General Gobillard and then back to the interpreter, when she spoke Serb, I had time to take a few notes, but I did not take very detailed notes. I drafted those up afterwards in consultation with General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you that in a moment. How soon after the events did you prepare the note that is now our exhibit?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly but I would say the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you discussed it with General Gobillard, did you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the note is in English rather than French for what reason?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was sent to other headquarters and it made it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you discussed these events with General Gobillard in the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never seen General Gobillard since.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now going to try and begin this process of analysing and comparing the two documents. If we could begin by looking at the actual intercept, 2379, we can see at the very top that what is coming from the Serb end are these words: "General Mladic is in the field and he too is away. I can only put him through to General Gvero if he wants. Please hold on. Hello, this is Gvero." So would I be right in saying that it appears that the person General Gobillard first wanted to speak to was General Mladic, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It also appears to be the position, doesn't it, that General Gvero was not specifically the person to whom General Gobillard wanted to speak and Gobillard was being told that in effect the only person available to field the conversation was Gvero. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could move, please, to the second paragraph in your note, second sentence of that paragraph, you note the following: "If UNPROFOR troops were really targeted, then it was the BiH who fired on to them according to their old scenario." In the intercept, 2379, about ten lines down, General Gvero seems to have said, "If UN members have been shot at, it was not by us. Rather following the familiar scenario, they were shot at by the Muslims who are very close to them and whom you are protecting." Did you have any idea what General Gvero was referring to when he used the expression, "familiar scenario"?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This came on occasions from our discussions with Serb side. They would accuse the Bosnians of provoking and to try to -- for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And UNPROFOR were aware of that, weren't they, the truth of that assertion by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware that on occasion, yes, it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at 6D204 in this regard. This is a daily sit-rep from General Janvier or at least from his office to, among others, New York and Mr. Annan, and I want to look at page 6, please. It's dated the 10th of July. We can see that at the fax heading at the top of that page. If we could scroll down, please, this is in a part of the document which is described as a military assessment of events in Srebrenica. So it's almost completely contemporaneous with your conversation, perhaps a day or so earlier, and it says, "Similar to what happened in Gorazde, spring 1994, the BiH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR, including the RRF, or NATO, into the conflict on BiH side. Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave or alarming reports from Bosnian side on the situation in the enclaves will be indicated for this." Do you know what the author of this report is referring to?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Spring 1994 was before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. But in short, you've already accepted you were aware -- you knew what General Gvero was driving at when he used the word "old scenario" or "familiar scenario"?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next bit I'd like to look at, please, is still on the first page of your document. Yes, perhaps we could go back to the two documents in B/C/S on e-court. Thank you. But in the hard copy that you've got, on that first page, we see it says, "The BSA were not attacking civilians either. They had fought against the BiH armed terrorists who should have been disarmed according to the agreement concluded by the parties under the auspices of UNPROFOR." If you could look, please, at the actual intercept, halfway down the first page, we see it says, "Next, we didn't shoot at civilians but at armed terrorists who have inflicted losses on our people in the last months and years. They were supposed to be disarmed according to the agreement we signed with them in the presence of the UN, but that was never done." So General Gvero juxtaposes the armed terrorists with people who have inflicted losses on our people, words - and let me emphasise this is not a criticism - but words which were not in your document, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand him to be saying at that point?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I knew at that time, but during that period I found out that the Bosnian army, in Zepa, for example, were conducting raids outside the enclave into Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. This exercise is going to take a fair bit longer, I'm afraid, Your Honour so perhaps now would be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the break now. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Colonel, bottom of your note, you say, page 1, this is, "UNPROFOR troops were most welcome on the BSA territory where they would be treated comfortably and would be completely safe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No broadcast of the two documents, okay? Or at least of 2379.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you understand General Gvero to be saying at that juncture in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they would not take us hostage like they had done at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you have any knowledge at that point in time of how the DutchBat troops, who were in Bratunac, had come to get there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we look at 6D22, please? Now, whilst this is got up on the screen, to explain to you, I appreciate this is a document you almost certainly have never seen before because it's a document from Major General Krstic, to the Main Staff of the VRS and to the Drina Corps command, and it's an interim combat report dated the 9th of July of 1995. And it's not quite on the screen yet. We see the B/C/S version on the right there. There is the English. And it's item number 4 that I would like us to examine. It says this: "Conduct of UNPROFOR forces, the UNPROFOR forces at the check-points in Slapovici village and Bucje [phoen] village surrendered fully to our forces with all their weapons and equipment and asked for our protection. Ten UNPROFOR soldiers from the UNPROFOR check-point in Bucje village have been sent to and accommodated in Milici, while five soldiers from the check-point in Slapovici have been accommodated in Bratunac. UNPROFOR forces from the base in Potocari village did not intervene at the check-points or attack our forces." Now, that appears to be the information that has been sent by the Drina Corps, namely General Krstic, to the VRS Main Staff where my client was stationed at that time. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware, at the time of the conversation with General Gvero, of the information contained in General Krstic's interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, if we may, please, to the second page of your notes of the telephone call. And about six or seven lines down in the second paragraph, you write the following: "He" obviously referring to General Gvero, "claimed that a great number of UN vehicles stolen by the BiH and still painted white were used against the BSA. He said he had no absolute knowledge of who the troops in the vehicles belonged to, but drew the general's attention to the BSA reliable information that those were the BiH." What was your state of knowledge, Colonel, at about 6.00 on the 11th of July of the assertions that General Gvero was making?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we did not have information that the BiH had stolen any of our vehicles. And I believe the Dutch were able to confirm that. But we did know that the VRS still had vehicles taken during the hostage crisis and that were not returned until later. For example, I personally obtained Canadian vehicles, eight armoured vehicles, taken during the hostage crisis by the VRS on December 24th, 1995, when I went to get them in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where, in the hostage crisis of May 1995, were these vehicles taken? Whereabouts, in Bosnia, were they seized?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around Sarajevo for the most part, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm right, it's May 1995, we're talking about, about six weeks before the events that this case is concentrating upon, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look in relation to what I've just shown you, at 6D23, please? This is a similar document to the one that I just showed you. It's another interim combat report, this time of the 10th of July from Krstic to the VRS Main Staff and the Drina Corps command. And it's paragraph 3 that I'd like to look at here, please. It says, "UNPROFOR conduct in the Srebrenica enclave, from observation and surveillance of the situation in the Srebrenica enclave, we concluded the number of UNPROFOR check-points on enemy territory had been taken by the Muslims who are using some of the weapons and other military hardware in operations against our forces." So on the face of this document, Krstic is telling his Main Staff that broadly speaking what General Gvero is asserting to you was, in fact, happening in the field, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You of course can't comment on the accuracy of General Krstic's document, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's hard to think of any reason why General Krstic would be misleading his Main Staff or falsifying this type of report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sounds fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Back to your report of the conversation, the last paragraph, you say, "General Gvero promised he would do his utmost to keep the situation in the region of Srebrenica under control, which he thought quite possible because of his competent military there." If we could look, please, in this regard at the actual intercept, second page, about ten lines up from the bottom, it says, "We'll do everything to keep the situation under control. We have competent people from our army." So it's fair to say that General Gvero wasn't personally promising to keep the situation under control. He was talking in the first person plural about the VRS in a general sense. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back to your document, and following on from where I had left off, you say, "What happened this day only served to complicate the situation in the region of Srebrenica, and would ill effect the situation there. He would have had the full insight into the situation in the Srebrenica area by the next morning." Going back, if we may, to the actual intercept, again a little on from where I had left off, it says, "It would be best to speak with General Gobillard in the morning and to look at the overall situation." In fact, what you have written is, I would suggest, not a completely fair summary because General Gvero was not suggesting that he would have a full insight into the situation in Srebrenica the following morning. He is simply saying that it would be best to speak the following morning, a subtle but significant difference, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Josse, because I think the words or the phrase, "He would have had the full insight" are reflected in the intercept in the part which reads as follows: "It would be best to speak with General Gobillard in the morning and to look at the overall situation," which I mean to look at the overall situation then, at that point in time. Because then in the witness's report, this is followed -- "That was why he suggested another contact by phone only next morning." And as you see that is not followed by what is contained in the intercept, which is reflected in the sentence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I just have a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've heard what the learned judge has just said, Colonel. And by all means, look at more of the intercept if it helps, but General Gvero doesn't appear to actually be saying that he would have a full insight into the situation in the Srebrenica area, isn't that fair?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't disagree that it is. From my point of view at the other end, it was not an important nuance at the time, the information that was conveyed was more important than how it was conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we look at the very end of the intercept, it's not -- again understandably -- reflected in whole in your summary. General Gvero says, "I would like General Gobillard to continue making reasonable decisions to not call in the air force, to make mistakes, and I want him to conclude his mission as a decent man and a man of peace, neutral, and impartial towards all sides in this conflict. Many thanks and good night." And you've summarised that as inviting Gvero inviting Gobillard to show no bias towards any party, as I've just indicated what in fact he said was rather fuller than that, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you basically dealt with this in your examination-in-chief with Mr. Thayer, but this conversation took place at about 10 minutes past 6.00 on the 11th of July, in the evening. There is no question that the aircraft who were providing the close air support had been withdrawn almost exactly an hour earlier. Do you agree with that? If you don't, I can help you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know they had been withdrawn shortly before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so, de facto, this conversation had no effect on the decision by UNPROFOR as to whether or not to bomb the VRS. That must be right, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now -- and one thing that I should have asked you at the very start of this conversation, and then I'll move away from it, it's obvious from the start that this was a telephone call that was put in from General Gobillard' office to the Main Staff of the VRS rather than the other way around, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, this conversation took place at the very tail end of the period when General Smith was away on leave. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you accept the criticism that during those 11 days, General Gobillard spent too much time in the PTT building and not enough time in the Residency?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying that General Smith was away for 11 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He was away from the 1st of July to the 11th of July. I think on the 8th of July he went it Geneva, but he did not return to Sarajevo until the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that on the 1st and 2nd of July, he was in Split and he retained command at that time, so there would have been no need because he was still in theatre, as we say it, there would have been no need for General Gobillard to be at BH command. But after that, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've got no view on the subject?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall other than the events we have been going through between the 8th of July and the 12th, I don't recall the specifics before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Gobillard had assumed control, notwithstanding that Nicolai was Smith's Chief of Staff; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's also right, and I'll tell you this in case you don't recall, that Smith was in daily contact with his military assistant, Colonel Baxter. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no, because I wasn't there all the time during that whole period that you mentioned, but that would be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in particular, when Smith went to Geneva on the 8th of July, do you recall any discussion in your circles, either with your general, i.e. Gobillard, or perhaps in the officer's mess at a slightly lower level, as to whether Smith should return bearing in mind he was in Geneva and had effectively left his leave?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall such discussion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you that is it might give some indication as to the extent to which you in UNPROFOR in Sarajevo had some sense of the impending crisis. Does that help at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't recall any such discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
