utterances.text: And are you able to help us at all as to who said what at the point that Smith was recalled from his leave on the 11th of July, who made that decision, whether you were party to any discussions, formal, informal, or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have been but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your witness statement, dealing really with this period of time, the time before the 11th of July, you said - and I could show this to you if need be - the difficulty was to get accurate information from Srebrenica and then deciding what to do.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, the situation was confused. We were getting information from the Dutch company through DutchBat and Sector north-east to BH command, from the GCO, British GCO, in Srebrenica directly to BH command, from civil affairs, from the Bosnians, from the Serbs, and of course it was not entirely clear what was happening, who was attacking the Dutch and at what location, and what we could do to prevent any further attacks or advance by the VRS. So all of that were of course from a distance being in Sarajevo and watching over events in Srebrenica. It was difficult to get a clear picture, something that we were sure this is what's happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at page 18 of your statement, talking specifically about the 10th of July, you use a very similar expression, "We were very unsure of their situation." Similar point, I assume?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been asked this morning about the death of the Dutch soldier, Renssen, and your recollection of those events. Do you recall what General Gobillard's official reaction to that event was?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was not happy about it and wanted a strong protest made to the Bosnians who had killed the Dutch soldier that this amounted to murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We know that General Janvier wrote to his counterpart, General Delic, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have been but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was General Gobillard's counterpart within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally it was Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But he was a civilian, wasn't he? He was a Prime Minister, he wasn't a military man at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I got the wrong name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akolov [phoen] Aznadzic at corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry give it us the name again?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's Aznadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to need some help on this. Either way, did General Gobillard express his outrage specifically to his counterpart about the death of Renssen?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- well, I say normally it was Aznadzic when we were operating at sector level. When he was acting commander UNPROFOR or BH command during that period, he would have had contacts at a higher level of the BiH army. I can't think of the name right now. Did he express that directly to that contact? I'm not sure if he did. He may have. But also General Nicolai was supposed to draft something so we could complain formally about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could it have been a military man called Hajrulahovic, I'm going to spell that H-A-J-R-U-L-A-H-O-V-I-C?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I believe he's the one we used to call Talijan because we couldn't pronounce his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Talijan. That's the man. Now, going to move on to the 28th of July or 27th, 28th of July, when you went to Zepa. Remind us, who did you go there with, please?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Chinouihl was the French engineer commander at Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on the 27th of July, General Smith was there. Your first day, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, for a short period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you describe both in your diary and to some extent in your witness statement of General Smith's departure. Excuse me a moment. Probably is worth having a look at this. Page 24 of the witness statement, which is 6D152. That's exactly the point that I want. We see that it says towards the top that General Smith arrived at 1550 and then going on down the page, it says, "General Smith talked to us, the UN people, before he left." And I'm not going to read all this out. You can read it to yourself. B/C/S page 22. In effect he was rallying his troops, for want of a better expression, General Smith, this is, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Making sure that those present understood what was at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, did you understand -- have you any idea, did General Smith return to Zepa at any point?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not that you're aware of. Did you get the impression that this was a rallying call before he left for a final time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I recall precisely, but it would have been not a situation report but a look at the situation as it is now, share the understanding, and then each carries his activities, not as a final -- not as a final rallying call, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Colonel Baxter with him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The questions I'm about to ask you are quite detailed, and I will understand if you do not recall but let's try. Do you recall whether he had one of his liaison officers-cum-interpreters with him at this meeting you described on page 24 of the statement?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've mentioned Captain Bliss. Do you recall the name of his other liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I mentioned name to you Captain Dibb, does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It doesn't. Was Captain Bliss in Zepa at any point when you were there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would Smith always, as far as you can recall, have one of his liaison officers with him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Digressing for a moment, how did General Gobillard deal with communication with the warring parties? Did he have a personal interpreter?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were they military officers?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both military and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you recall, did -- who accompanied him on the trip to Zepa on the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have to be one of his military. Either Major Beck or Korsek [phoen], I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Both French officers, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legionnaires. They were senior NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Help us -- you've use used this expression "legionnaire" before. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the French Foreign Legion is a unit of the French army mainly composed of soldiers from foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've made clear, and certainly not disputing this, Smith leaves on the 27th of July and Gobillard arrives on the 28th of July. Would it be a deliberate decision for any one of them to be in Zepa at any given time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning their own choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, not so much their own choice but would there be some sort of informal policy decision that one wouldn't send two such senior generals to a place like Zepa on the same day at the same time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. They are commanders operating at two different levels. So commander Sector Sarajevo had responsibilities for Zepa and as did commander UNPROFOR who had responsibilities for all of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on, you say in the witness statement, it's there in front of us, at the next paragraph, that Smith left Ed Joseph from civil affairs behind. Who else from UNPROFOR did he leave? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Mr. Bezrouchenko? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he had been there earlier. I don't know if he was still there or if he left. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as a matter of interest, I take it you haven't had a chance to discuss this with Mr. Bezrouchenko. I say that because he works in this building. Are you able to -- have you spoken to him about it at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact I've never seen him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that he worked in this building?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What time did you depart Zepa on the 28th of July? As accurately as you can, please. This is particularly important.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in my diary. After the meeting General Gobillard had with General Tolimir towards the late afternoon, but I don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I think we can remain in open session. The diary simply says that you returned to check-point 2 and met Gobillard at about 1600 hours. "He met Tolimir, and then I left Zepa to return with him to Sarajevo." So the question is how long did the meeting with Tolimir take, between Gobillard and Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At all? This is particularly important, Colonel, actually.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guess but I really don't recall how long it could have taken, but I think I'm more precise in my diary as to when the meeting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I just said.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, you're more precise in your note. I think you say in your note which is the handwritten note which was a Prosecution Exhibit, I think you say 1710. We are just going to find a copy. I haven't got it to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can agree that 2969 indicates that this meeting was 28 July at 1720 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So your handwritten note says the meeting appears to have started at 1720 as Mr. Thayer has helpfully just said, and you don't recall how long it took?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but certainly less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you and your general then immediately turned around and went back to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the point that you left, was there any sign of General Smith in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea when, if at all, General Smith next went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, in fact, your diary says that the journey took four hours, the return journey to Sarajevo. That sounds about right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, which is much faster than 20 some hours it took the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's because you were held up in Rogatica, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the -- any recollection about what you did about food that evening? I only ask to see if it perhaps jogs your memory as to what time you left or where you ate or what time you ate, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't -- I don't recall any more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I take it there was no sign of General Gvero in Zepa on either the 27th or the 28th of July, was there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, having never met him, I couldn't have recognised him any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. And there was no suggestion from any of the VRS troops that there was another general there amongst them, Tolimir in particular?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few things about matters that you mentioned in your evidence-in-chief, and you gave some evidence about fuel and the fact that you had become aware that the Ukrainian Brigade were trading fuel with the Serbs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The Ukrainian company in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And where had that information come from, please?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact source, just something that was discussed at sector headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there was no intelligence or information that the Bosniak inhabitants were doing the same, namely trading fuel with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say it's possible, it's possible it happened, it's possible there was some information, what, please?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both actually. Both are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've a low opinion of that company, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the unit, as I described yesterday, in general, was having lots of problems and not behaving very professionally in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to be perfectly fair about this, if I can confronted you with suggestions that the local inhabitants were trading in fuel with that Ukrainian company, you've already said it wouldn't come as a surprise to you at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. You said this about that company, that there were suspicions that they were pro-Serb. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm. I also said that this -- these suspicions were expressed by French officers at the headquarters Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have a view on the subject?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, it was easier for them to move about in Serb-held territory than for anybody else except perhaps the Russians after the hostage crisis of May 1995. In fact, we could not for a while go into Serb-held territory, the weeks following the hostage crisis, but we had to maintain contact with Indic, for example, in Lukavica, and we would use the Ukrainians to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you have any information about how the Ukrainians interacted with the population of Zepa, particularly as the crisis was brewing?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no details anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 6D122, please. We need page 5 of the English, please, and page 5 of the B/C/S. This, let me tell you, Colonel, to cut matters short, is a document that emanates from February of 1996, and it's a review by a Brigadier General Jasarevic of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa. And in the middle of that page, we see him talking about the Chetniks' attack on Zepa on the 9th of July of 1995. He talks about the local brigade, the 285th Light Brigade, and he talks about the Ukrainians. And then he says, about halfway through that paragraph, "After the commander of this UNPROFOR battalion crossed over to the command of the Chetnik forces, the new Ukrainian Battalion commander handed over all weapons at its disposal to our soldiers. These were immediately used to defend Zepa. According to several displaced persons from Zepa, he even sent false reports to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo saying that members of the Ukrainian Battalion had been directly attacked and requesting NATO air strikes against the Chetniks." So in short, this is in effect Muslim intelligence, which is being reproduced in a Muslim report. Can you comment on this at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first I hear of this, and frankly it seems a bit far-fetched.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the information that I had and what I knew of the Ukrainians, as I said, they were not the best of soldiers, but going so far as to lie to their command? I doubt that. That's my personal appraisal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Bosniaks, around the 15th, 16th of July, asked for air strikes on the VRS because of their offensive against Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You remember that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not sure about the dates you're mentioning, but we had some, let's say, complaints from the Bosnians, requesting that we do something, namely air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Last question on this: These French officers felt, for reasons that you've explained, that the Ukrainians were pro-Serb. If the Ukrainians were pro-Serb, were the rest of UNPROFOR pro-Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it would mean that they were more impartial, as the UN would like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you see any part of UNPROFOR, I know it's a large organisation, that you would categorise as pro-Muslim?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't comment about every individuals but organisation, I don't think so, or I haven't been a witness to things like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll deal with this vis-a-vis your diary in a moment, but would you categorise General Smith as more pro-Bosniak than your commander, General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to go through various extracts in your journal. Before we go into private session to do that, bearing in mind you were asked some general questions about it in open session, I think I can ask you this at the moment: The journal, as you made clear, was actually compiled in late 1997, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was put together as it is, yes, but as I said, all the meetings that I attended and where I took notes, those notes were typed usually the same day or in a relatively short time, and when I produced the journal they were cut and paste, put all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were they private notes or were they notes which formed some part of an official UNPROFOR archive?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many portions of it were documents that I had written as reports, and we've seen some of them here in the last couple of days, but a lot was personal as well. So it's a mix of both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And those personal notes that you had, you've told us, you've destroyed after you put the journal together, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why did you put the journal together? What was the purpose, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a tidy individual. I'd like to have everything neatly in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go to private session?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been asked -- you've been asked in part by both my learned friends who preceded me for other defendants in this case about the spring offensive, and about the BiH attack on the Serbs around Sarajevo, and that offensive broke the cessation of hostilities agreement, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have explained that UNPROFOR took exception to the fact that the Serbs took heavy weapons from the weapons collection points, and as a result NATO decided to bomb the VRS, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look at the situation in the eastern enclaves, if we may. The VRS were on the offensive there, weren't they? They started the attack. And the ABiH were on the defensive, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- you mean at Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for this purpose, in fact, we only need to concern ourselves with Srebrenica. The ABiH took weapons from the weapon collection point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly I don't recall. That was before -- if it happened, and it might have, that was before we got involved at BH command level. We meaning General Gobillard and I. So I don't remember that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you don't remember that happening at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How, then, were the local inhabitants able to put up any defence at all?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, heavy weapons and other weapons plus everything they could have hidden in such a large area. One of the reasons these three enclaves in the east existed was because there were not -- the VRS was not able to capture them initially. They had enough forces and weapons and the terrain, the terrain was very difficult. And it was very costly to send troops in there to try and dislodge armed people, even lightly armed people. So I suspect that's how it happened. They had their own rifles, possibly had hidden armaments as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's a few minutes early. Perhaps we could take the break. I haven't got very long at all but I would appreciate a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you will have a few minutes left in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I mean a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There will be limited re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for those minutes, Your Honour, because in fact, I had left out one important matter in relation to the Gobillard-Gvero conversation and so could those two documents be put back up on e-court in B/C/S, please? So far as those of us who have the hard copy are concerned in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to take you, if I may, Colonel, to the second page and the third paragraph. The second paragraph, I beg your pardon. And the sentence at the very end where you record General Gvero as saying "He even added that BiH civilians once on the BSA territory would be totally safe and were welcome to leave the enclave." I would suggest that the comparative bit in the actual intercept is also on page 2, in the middle of the page, where General Gvero says, "Svetlana, tell him this as well. General, the refugees who come over to our side will be totally safe. We will protect those civilians, and they can come over to our side and they will be safe. That's it." It doesn't appear, does it, that General Gvero makes any reference at all to these civilians leaving the enclave. Would you agree with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read that. I don't get your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the point is, in your summary, you used the words, "And were welcome to leave the enclave." Gvero, in the actual intercept, talks about protecting the civilians and that they can come over to our side, but he doesn't say anything about them leaving the enclave as such, does he?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, again it may be --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's understandable and it may be a subtle difference and it may be a difference without a distinction. That's a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide in due course. But the proposition I'm putting to you is correct, he doesn't mention leaving the enclave as such, does he?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to go back into private session again in one moment's time. The diary which we've seen a little bit of is an extensive document. It of course deals with the crisis in the eastern enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa particularly, in July, but it deals with a lot of other events as well, a lot of the other concerns that Sector Sarajevo had, in particular, for example the Igman route that we touched on earlier?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you in your sector had a lot of other concerns, there were -- the war was taking place in areas other than in the east, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there was much to keep you and your general busy aside from the eastern enclaves, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we very briefly go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Final document that I want to show you is 6D132, which the Trial Chamber has seen before; you may have done 12 years ago. It's an UNPROFOR report of the 17th of July, and it describes events in Gorazde between the 15th and 16th of July. I won't read it out because it's been read to the Trial Chamber before, but perhaps you'd like to read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this is the tail end of the Srebrenica crisis. The middle of the Zepa crisis. And the Bosniaks in Gorazde are behaving in a way which can be mildly -- described mildly as difficult towards the Ukrainians in that particular enclave. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw that report actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did -- Gorazde fell under Sector Sarajevo, in other words, Gobillard's responsibility, correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did he deal with this?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the face of it, quite serious, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you've no recollection as to how the sector dealt with this and secured the Ukrainians and made sure the Bosniaks started to behave themselves again?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for all your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer, I take it you have a short cross-examination -- re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As short as possible, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to pick up on that last point, Colonel, and good afternoon to you again, you've heard some questions about attempts by Muslims in now all the enclaves to get their hands on whatever weapons they could during these attacks. What was your understanding as to why they were so desperate to get their hands on those weapons, that they would overrun peacekeepers' OPs?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had resisted attacks early on in the war, attacks that resulted in the creation of those enclaves, because the VRS could not take them. Now they saw the new pressure at that time by the VRS to reduce or recapture the enclaves, as the ultimate attempt to get rid of those enclaves, and I guess they wanted to resist at all cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked some follow-up questions concerning the reports you received of the Ukrainian company soldiers trading in fuel with the Serbs. Can you enlighten the Trial Chamber a little bit about what amounts we are talking about here? Are we talking about enough to fill a chain saw or are we talking about other amounts?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly I don't recall the exact amounts, but what gave us -- or attracted our attention was the fact that it was fairly large amounts, amounts to be able to drive vehicles some distances or run them for hours or...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, to save time I'm not going to show you a series of documents, but if the BSA or if the VRS attacked an OP, peace keeper check-point, OP or other position, with tank fire or mortars or similarly targeted a civilian population or position or building, would that justify the use of close air support?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they attacked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a question that requires speculation because the situation was what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that requires any speculation. If we are talking about a situation where a UN position, be it an OP or a check-point, has come under fire, by mortar or tank, is that a violation that justified the use of close air support? This witness has been asked many questions of a similar nature that require no more speculation than what I am asking this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is no speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just have to wait for the Trial Chamber to confer. Mr. President, the witness answered the question while the Chamber was conferring. I don't think he understood what was -- what the huddle meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have our headphones on because we were conferring at the time. But in any case, our decision is that it is a perfectly legitimate question because it falls within the rules of engagement with which supposedly the witness was familiar. So let's proceed. In any case he's answered it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may take a look at 2968, please? And if the Chamber still has both versions, both the intercept and the original I would invite Your Honours to look at both, but it's not entirely necessary for the purposes of my questions. Colonel, let me know when you have your report of the 11th of July Gobillard-Gvero conversation on your screen and if you've got a hard copy, okay. And I'll just wait until the English is actually up on e-court before proceeding. Okay. Then I'll just proceed. Colonel, turning your attention to the second paragraph on the first page of this document, where you have written that General Gvero said, and I'll invite the Chamber to check the intercept as well, "Our army never attacked UNPROFOR." Sir, based on your state of knowledge at this time on the 11th of July, was that a true statement by General Gvero or a false statement by General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a false statement. We knew that what the VRS move on to the pocket created the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we move further in this document, where you have written, "BSA -- " this is according to General Gvero, "BSA were not attacking civilians either." Based on your state of knowledge sir at that time, was General Gvero's statement true or false?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: False. There had been some shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And turning to the next page, sir, General Gvero's statement to you that "A great number of UN vehicles stolen by the BiH and still painted white were used against the BSA," was that a true statement or a false statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: False, in our view, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, how would you describe General Gvero's state of knowledge of the events on the ground based on your recollection of this conversation? How would you describe his state or degree of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hang on. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I ask rhetorically how can he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very simple, Mr. President. Based on his recollection of what General Gvero was saying during this conversation, based on the issues that General Gvero addressed during the conversation, based on the positions that General Gvero took in this conversation, what was your understanding or how would you describe General Gvero's state of knowledge of the events on the ground based on your participation in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a question for you, not for the witness, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, if at the time you did form in your mind an assessment of whether General Gvero basically knew what he was talking about or not, then please proceed to answer the question. If not, we don't want you to go back now and speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said earlier in my testimony, during this period, 9, 10, 11 July, we believed that the Serbs were basically always repeating the party line, if I may, and they were stalling tactics. While it created confusion on our part, it delayed us in taking actions, it allowed them more time to press on and move on to the pocket. So this example of General Gvero and some of the things that he said is more of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, Colonel, just to follow up on His Honour's question, did you form in your mind an assessment at the time of whether General Gvero knew what he was talking about and knew what he was doing in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this conversation, sir, did you gain any impression as to whether General Gvero was sidelined or marginalised in any form in terms of his authority or role on the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the impression I had. He was like the others we had been talking to, using the same stalling tactics, creating confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to be given leave to ask the Lieutenant-Colonel a question that came out of my learned friend's redirects specifically on page 79, which was the justification, I think, for the close air strikes that we discussed moments ago. And the question, if you want me to put it to the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should I put it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No tell us what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question is basically if it's true that close air strikes are justified on an attack on an OP, observation post, or a check-point, why did not UNPROFOR at any time order much less consider such strikes when the Bosnian Muslims attacked both the observation posts and the check-points both in Srebrenica and in Zepa in July of 1995 as we've heard from his evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you wish to comment on that? Do you have any objection to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I think that's a fair question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Ostojic. You've put the question, I suppose the Colonel can proceed to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir you've heard the question, but if you'd like me to rephrase it, I can rephrase it for you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it's clear. And the occasion where we discussed where the BiH army attacked directly UNPROFOR, it justified -- meets the criteria for using close air support. It was just not practical to do so because our troops and there -- we would have been firing on our own hand, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify if I may, Mr. President, my question had two parts to it: Ordering it and or considering it. Through looking at your notes and the documents we have from the various UNPROFOR entities, it never seemed to be considered, sir. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we can say it was never considered but the using it was a totally impractical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Colonel, we've come to the end of your testimony. We don't have any further questions for you, which means you will be flying back home soon. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this trial, and we all wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Exhibits? Mr. Thayer? We haven't got a list. Or an updated list. How come?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no explanation. I'd be happy to stand next to my friend and share it with him, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's your influence, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right. We have four -- I'm sorry, five new exhibits, 2968 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment let me follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this should track the list of exhibits that we had tendered or that we had distributed in advance of Colonel Fortin's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to have a clear picture of what you're tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll recite them, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just the 65 ter number, these.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 2968, 2969, 2970, 2502, and 6D00165. That is the journal. I expect that we may have to have some discussions about once again putting the whole thing in evidence or just putting in the portions that were referred to. My preference would be just put the whole thing in with all the translations that accompany it and whatever sections are needed to be referred to in the future, everybody can do that without having to create three separate documents, which is what we would have to do, one from the original French, one from the English translation, and one from the B/C/S. This way I just think it will be more efficient and a simpler process to offer the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections? Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for point of clarification I'm not sure in my index what is right off the top, 2502.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise. We had initially thought that that was not a document that had been used before. It was in fact MFI'd in connection with Mr. Torlak's testimony. So I think we had initially given that the number 2971. We went back and found out that it originally had been assigned 2502. That is the 15 July Harland report that I believe at least one of my friends also used during their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that clear enough, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our preference, Your Honour, would be for the selected passages of the diary to be admitted into evidence. I am bound to say that I would have no objection to the whole diary going into evidence if we had some assurance from the Trial Chamber that they would only rely upon those passages that had in some way been alluded to during the course of the case. It's a point I've made before. Basically we submit we need to know partly the evidence that we've got to meet in the trial but more to the point the evidence that is going to be considered when the Trial Chamber comes to deliberate at the end of this trial. Whilst it will be rather cumbersome for the four parties or three parties who have cross-examined on the document, the one party who examined in chief in relation to it, my preference would be that we do produce a separate document with those passages that have been dealt with during the course of the various examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just let me make explicit what I thought was implicit in my submission a few moments ago which is we do trust the Trial Chamber to do exactly that and not roam where the witnesses have not taken us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position -- I think -- is no different from the position that we have taken already in the past on similar instances, and that is that for us it will be much easier if we are to follow, to have the entire document, especially if we are to establish dates and sequence. But the understanding obviously is that we will be relying only for the purposes of our deliberations on the parts that you have made use of during the testimony of this Colonel, and during the testimony of others if it's the case, and nothing beyond that. So again, our preference is to have the full document rather than excerpts from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, of course, it's your decision, but could I say we are quite happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the -- to make things easier and clearer for both of you, I mean, if you come forward and indicate the parts on which you are relying, it will be even much better for us because we will have a straightforward direction from -- indication from you. All right. Any objections as regards the other documents, Prosecution documents? None. So they are admitted. This diary will go under seal. The diary will go under seal because of the restrictions that we spoke about in an earlier sitting. Yes, Mr. Thayer? I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to advise the Chamber that we have no objections to any of the documents that had been tendered by any of the teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To my knowledge there is only one. Mr. Josse, there is only one document to my knowledge that you wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, even though it's previously been referred to we had never actually tendered it, as far as our records can see. We would now like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That to confirm is 6D132?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection I take it and no objection from any of the other Defence teams? So that document is admitted. No documents, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that concludes the Louis Fortin's testimony. Is the next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, our next witness is here. Mr. McCloskey had an issue to address with the Court prior that that might -- okay. Well, we'll finish this issue, then. We do have the next witness available. If I might propose something, given that we have Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination still to go, which I think is estimated at a half an hour, and we have additional cross-examination from Madam Fauveau, I would suggest that given the final preliminary, it may not be worth bringing him -- bringing the witness in to get only half of one of those two cross-examinations done and then pick it up on another day. If the Court feels that that's useful, to pick it up and get at least half of one, then okay, but I just note that it may just be easier to keep him as a gap filler for another rainy day and get both cross-examinations done in one fell swoop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But that may sound okay when it relates to Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination, even though we don't know whether he will finish it in 20 minutes, but we had an indication from Madam Fauveau earlier on that she could conclude her further cross examination in 20 minutes. So if there is no objection, we could do that with Mr. Blaszczyk, provided he can show up without delay. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I just want to inform you that this will be even shorter, I think five minutes will be even plenty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask whether my colleague from the OTP has a hard copy of the document coming from the Republic of Serbia. For technical reasons we didn't have time to upload it into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. So I take it we can tell General Nicolai to go away, to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, when you said the next witness, I thought you meant the gap filler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General Nicolai is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's why -- I thought he was here and I was telling you to tell him that he can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Lost in some translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to respond to Ms. Fauveau. I'm sorry, I don't have an extra hard copy of that document. We spoke earlier and maybe she has one now and I offered to provide one and maybe we misunderstood, but she told me she could print one herself she thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you but I solved the problem. I found hard copies, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's wait for Mr. Blaszczyk. And Mr. Ostojic, how much time do you think you require for -- to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do think about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek wouldn't tell us last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think a half hour, Your Honour. I think I indicated last time on the 2nd of November I had about an hour, but looking at it I do really believe I have an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: An hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I mean a half hour or so. Not an hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, since the Prosecution motion to add to their 65 ter list in relation to this witness that I mentioned to you earlier on, may become urgent, sort of, if we get Mr. Blaszczyk back to testify soon. I would like you to respond to it by not later than Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for your information, good afternoon, we had agreed to discuss the matter after court today ourselves, and so I think we will probably be able to work that out between us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm asking is to come back to us with final position by Monday morning and then we see what is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back, we don't need to repeat the solemn declaration procedure. It's still valid, and you're testifying pursuant to it. Madam Fauveau has some further questions to put to you after which we will adjourn and then you will need to come back again. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to give the witness a document 5D533. Unfortunately it has not been uploaded into e-court yet. In the meanwhile, while you are waiting for the document, I'd like to recall part of your cross-examination dated November 22nd. I asked you whether the documents between Mali Zvornik and Gornji Milanovac could be somewhere else. You answered on page 18107, line 14 to 16, "[In English] I cannot exclude that possibility, but we received information from the government of Serbia. They were mentioned only transportation of this collection from Mali Zvornik to Gornji Milanovac. Nothing more." [Interpretation] The document that I just handed you is a document that comes from the Republic of Serbia. It is the only document of -- from the Republic of Serbia that we have. Is this the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that this document mentions -- makes no mention of transfer from Mali Zvornik to Gornji Milanovac? Maybe you can just look at it. It's not a very long document. Could you please read it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This document mentioned only Mali Zvornik. When that archive was transferred to Mali Zvornik and refers also only to the place where -- we can -- we can assume it refers to the place where the archive was handed over to the commission from Republika Srpska, but we know that -- we know from other statements that the place where the archive was handed over to Republika Srpska commission, it is Gornji Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't doubt this but we have no document proving that the documents were transferred from Mali Zvornik directly to Gornji Milanovac?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I think we don't have any further need for -- do you think there is an area that you could cover in ten minutes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- there always is actually, Your Honour, so if you want I can cover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to cover in your testimony on the 2nd of November when I was asking you questions, I covered an area which was called the chain of custody, and you answered on page 17438 the importance of the chain of custody, but I really didn't understand your answer. And I'll read it to you, and again it's page 17438. And you state on line 20 through 21, "Of course this is important," and we are talking about the chain of custody, "Because we can show, we can see if anybody interfere into these documents." My question to you is I don't understand that answer fully and can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Having the evidence, we would like to prove, we would like to show the Trial Chamber the way how the evidence was taken by us and also to show the way how, if it is possible, of course, how the evidence was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you use the word "interfere." Are you trying to perhaps say that you want to establish if anybody was able to manipulate or had access to somehow distort the documents as well, sir, as opposed to how the evidence was established?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is one -- yeah, it's also chain of custody information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that's critical and important as well, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well share with the Trial Chamber and me, if you will, what it is that you as the lead investigator in the last year and a half and being the second in charge during the course of this seizure of documents, what it is that you did to determine whether or not anybody, as you put it, interfered with the documents during the now 12 years since they were initially purportedly created?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't the second in charge of this course of the seizure. At that time, I just establish how we received these documents from Republika Srpska to our field office in Banja Luka, and then to our field office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think I understand the answer, sir, respectfully to you. Now, since you are in charge, did you go back to determine since it's important or critical, as we've said, to determine the veracity of those documents, what did you do or uncover that the Prosecution did while you were the team investigator and even before you, to determine whether these documents were authentic and that no one interfered with them, as you so put it?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: I tried to collect as much as possible information how this collection came to our possession, and also during the witnesses, during my investigation, we showed few of these documents to our witnesses, and they confirm that the documents were this collection are authentical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say our witnesses, you're talking about OTP witnesses?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about OTP witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, does the OTP have in-house witnesses such as a handwriting expert, for example?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, not in-house but we use the handwriting expert, but I think we used this handwriting experts but in regards to documents who came from this collection but was not seized in Banja Luka at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, which handwriting expert did you use or experts in order to determine that nobody interfered with this collection? We are talking now, I know you always wants to go back to Banja Luka, but we are talking about specifically here it's my understanding is your testimony is limited to the Drina Corps collection?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: But if we consider that documents received by the witness who testified in this Court, I think (redacted), we used the handwriting expert to confirm the authentication of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just quickly sir, in the moment that we have, did you go to a document reconstruction expert to determine if there was a manipulation or a distortion or additions or modifications or alterations made on any of the documents?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you use or at any time -- I think it's called a holographic or an ink and document specialist in order to confirm whether there were any add-ons made in the documents from the Drina Corps collection?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to --

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not both with respect to the document reconstruction expert and the ink and paper expert? If it's important and we think that it's critical to determine if there is this interference with the documents, why didn't you utilise those types of experts?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: These documents seems for us that -- to be authentical documents. We don't see any reason to use this type of expert at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But given that the documents were in the possession of (redacted) for approximately a year from the end of April or beginning of May 1998, through March of 199 -- end of March of 1999, did that cause any concern to you or any members of the Office of the Prosecution that the documents were in his sole position, and he was the only individual who maintained custody of those documents and was the only person who had keys for the padlocks where the documents were held?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Same objection as last time. I don't want to upset my friend again, but our position is he is misstating the evidence there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which part, Mr. Nicholls? Because Mr. Ostojic mentioned about six or seven different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: About the sole custody being this individual that he mentioned for this entire period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ostojic, do you wish to comment on that or do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No I don't accept it. I do not accept it at all, Your Honour. I don't know, he's referring to upsetting me on the last time. I think the question last time was related to Zvornik and Mali Zvornik. I think this witness has reviewed the statement by Nebojsa Vukcevic, if I'm saying it correctly, and clearly in that statement it identifies exactly who maintained the keys to that storage area, where the documents were, and who had sole possession of that. And there were two pad locks on the door, it's a statement that he relied on previously on the 2nd of November, so I think it's inaccurate to suggest that it misstates the facts. It does not misstate the facts whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. Sir, you've reviewed the statement that was given by Nebojsa Vukcevic did you not, May 2004?

utterances.speaker: Tomasz Blaszczyk (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that statement, sir, he states on the first page in the lower portion of the document, he states, that at the time chief of security organ of the 503rd Motorised Brigade was assigned to transfer the documentation to Mali Zvornik, and the transfer the of the archive from Zvornik to Mali Zvornik was supervised personally by the then-commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade, the individual whom we referenced, after the transfer the archive was placed in a small room at the above-mentioned border post which had no window and metal bars on the door. After placing the above-mentioned documentation in the above-mentioned room, it was sealed off locked with two padlocks and the keys were kept what Lieutenant-Colonel -- that individual's name, who was responsible for the storage of it in the above-mentioned place. March 23, 19 -- March 23rd, 1999, I was assigned by the 5th Corps Deputy Colonel Andric to go together with Lieutenant Savic to Mali Zvornik to find some documents. It then goes on let me just find the specific cite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you have a question ready or unless you want to repeat the question because our time is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll reconvene tomorrow. Tomorrow we will be sitting in the afternoon, as you recall. We have to move that. So it will be tomorrow at 2.15. And we start with the next witness. Thank you.
